title_patterns: [NAMED EXPERT/INSTITUTION]: [specific index or price level], then [specific qualifying counter-move]
[MARKET INSTRUMENT] just hit [precise level] — highest/lowest since [specific dated reference point]
Insiders bought [exact aggregate dollar figure] of these [N] stocks — [N-1] of them are in one sector
[N] stocks trading below [specific valuation metric] right now — screened, not recommended
What [specific earnings report] actually said vs what the [price move %] implied
[Time span] of [strategy] in [duration] — the [N] positions that carried the return
The [specific mechanism/plumbing term] behind this week's [instrument] move, explained with the actual data
[Policy or Treasury action] in plain numbers: what changed, what it costs, who pays
hook_patterns: Open with the single hardest number and its source in the first sentence, then state what it does NOT mean
Name the exact date/level of the last comparable reading before offering any interpretation
State the market's reaction (%) first, then immediately separate it from the underlying fundamentals
Lead with the disclosed filing or transcript line, quote it verbatim, then walk the math
Pose the question the price action raises, then say up front which parts the data can and cannot answer
packaging_notes: Two clear duration sweet spots: 5-9 min single-topic explainers (highest ratio-per-minute) and 18-30 min multi-name analysis; 45-90 min only works with named guests or documented case studies.
Unrounded and dated specifics outperform round scary numbers — '30-year yields highest since [year]' and exact insider dollar amounts travel further than percentage doom framing.
Named-authority framing (analyst, CEO filing, court document, earnings transcript) does heavy lifting; the source itself is the credibility hook, so put the name or document type in the title.
Two-part titles with a counterweight ('X, then Y' / 'this, not that') read as analysis rather than prediction and fit the no-hype position better than one-directional calls.
Earnings and macro-event windows drive most outliers — publish within 24-48h of the print or Treasury/Fed action, and let the title reference the event, not an emotion.
Screening/mechanism angles (insider buys, valuation screens, bond market plumbing) are the ethical replacement for crash bait: same curiosity gap, zero fear framing.
market_patterns.title: outlier pattern extraction

winning_patterns.pattern: Two-clause contradiction titles: a concrete outcome in clause one, then a clause that undercuts the obvious explanation for it
winning_patterns.structure: [entity] [directional move + exact %] + [but/while/not/still clause that denies the assumed cause]
winning_patterns.evidence: Our highest hook-hold and avg-view-pct videos (retention 80-114%, hook index 1.19-1.49) all pair a move with a reversal or qualifier clause; single-clause descriptive titles cluster at 45-65% retention.
winning_patterns.why_it_works: The second clause creates an open question the viewer needs the video to close, so the hook window is spent resolving tension instead of restating the title.

winning_patterns.pattern: One precise, unrounded number as the title's anchor — a percent, a price, or a day count
winning_patterns.structure: exactly one hard figure carried to a decimal or an exact integer, attached to one named ticker or person
winning_patterns.evidence: Best-retaining videos each carry a single sharp figure (a decimal percent, an exact day count). Titles built on a round dollar amount with no named subject retained 29-45%.
winning_patterns.why_it_works: A specific figure signals the video contains verifiable data, while a round dollar figure with no subject reads as generic and gives the hook nothing to prove.

winning_patterns.pattern: Disclosure-lag framing in the congress franchise: make the delay itself the subject, not the trade
winning_patterns.evidence: Within the congress franchise, versions that foreground the reporting delay hit 88-103% avg view and hook indexes of 1.21-1.36, while versions that foreground the thesis or the asset type sat at 63-76%.
winning_patterns.why_it_works: The lag implies something was withheld from the viewer, which is a grievance hook; the trade thesis alone is just information.

winning_patterns.pattern: Timing-collision framing: place two events next to each other and let the proximity do the work
winning_patterns.structure: [move or rally] + [adjacent event: notice, filing, split, lawsuit] + [tight time marker like '48 hours' or 'right as']
winning_patterns.evidence: Videos pairing a large percentage move with a delisting notice, a split date, or simultaneous legal filings retained 61-114% with hook indexes at or above 0.98.
winning_patterns.why_it_works: Adjacency in time implies causation the viewer wants confirmed or denied, which is a question the hook can answer immediately.

winning_patterns.pattern: Named-person subjects drive views; contradiction structure drives retention — the two levers are separate
winning_patterns.structure: recognizable name in the subject slot for reach + contradiction or lag clause for hold
winning_patterns.evidence: Our top-view videos (128-236) all lead with a recognizable name, but view rank does not track retention rank; the highest-retaining videos were low-view and structure-driven.
winning_patterns.why_it_works: The name earns the click from browse; only the structural tension keeps the viewer past the first 30%.

losing_patterns.structure: ['Stock Market Today' + calendar date] + [one unrelated example appended]
losing_patterns.evidence: The single long video collapsed to 12.3% avg view with a hook index of 0.31 — by far our worst on both measures.
losing_patterns.fix: Ship the strongest single item from the day as a short with a contradiction clause instead of bundling the day under a date.

losing_patterns.pattern: First-person production framing that makes the channel the subject
losing_patterns.evidence: Titles built around our own reading or reviewing process retained 17% despite belonging to the otherwise strong congress franchise.
losing_patterns.fix: Put the entity and the anomaly in the subject slot; never make our workflow the promise.

losing_patterns.pattern: Subject-less dollar amounts as the lead
losing_patterns.structure: [$ figure] + [vague transformation or consequence, no named ticker]
losing_patterns.evidence: Titles opening with a round dollar sum and no identified company retained 29-45%, among our weakest non-long videos.
losing_patterns.fix: Name the ticker or person first, then attach the figure as the anomaly.

losing_patterns.pattern: Broad-market vs single-actor comparisons where neither side carries a specific number
losing_patterns.evidence: This shape retained 31% with no measurable hook lift, while a structurally similar title that quoted an exact index percentage alongside an exact stock percentage held 53.7%.
losing_patterns.fix: If contrasting a stock against the market, put a hard figure on both sides of the contrast.

notes: Sample is thin — 20 videos, most under 100 views — so treat these as directional. The only high-confidence signals are the long-form roundup failure and the disclosure-lag framing within the congress franchise.
The congress franchise reliably wins views but its retention swings from 17% to 103% purely on title structure, meaning the franchise buys the click and the structure keeps the viewer.
Retention above 100% on several shorts indicates rewatching on tight, single-fact videos — a reason to keep runtimes short rather than expand into recap formats.
